title: Snapshot Registry
statement: Design a configuration registry that remembers history. set(key, value, time) records that key had value from time onward. get(key, time) returns the value that was current at that time: the value from the set with the largest time <= time for that key, or an empty string if there was none. Calls arrive as ["set", key, value, time] or ["get", key, time]; set times strictly increase across all calls, but get times can be anything. Return the result of every get, in order.
constraints: keys and values are 1–10 lowercase letters

examples.explanation: Before 5 nothing was set; from 5 to 8 it is dark; from 9 on it is light.
A key that was never set returns an empty string.

hints.content: Group history by key: each key has its own list of (time, value) pairs.
Because set times only increase, each key's list is already sorted by time.
A get asks for the last entry whose time is <= the query time.
That is an upper-bound binary search on the key's times.
Find the first index whose time is greater than the query; the answer is the entry just before it, or '' if that index is 0.

testCases.explanation: Before 5 nothing was set; from 5 to 8 it is dark; from 9 on it is light.
A key that was never set returns an empty string.
Lookups between, on and around recorded times.
A later set does not change the answer for an earlier time.
A long history queried at many times.

solutions.title: Scan all sets for each get
solutions.intuition: The answer is the latest matching set at or before the query time.
solutions.approach: Store every set. For each get, scan them and keep the best one with the same key and time <= query.
solutions.pseudocode: for op: set → sets.push; get → best = latest (k, v, t) with k == key and t <= time; out.push(best ? v : '')
commonMistakes: Returning the most recent set regardless of the query time.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A linear scan over history is correct but every lookup touches every set ever made.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: get theme 4: no set with time <= 4 → ''.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: get theme 8: dark@5 qualifies, light@9 does not → dark.

solutions.title: Per-key history with binary search
solutions.intuition: Each key's history is append-only and sorted by time, which is exactly what binary search needs.
solutions.approach: Keep a class with a Map from key to parallel arrays of times and values. set appends. get binary-searches for the first time > query and returns the value just before it.
solutions.pseudocode:
set(k, v, t): hist[k].times.push(t); hist[k].values.push(v)
get(k, t): i = first index with times[i] > t; return i ? values[i-1] : ''
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) per set, O(log h) per get
commonMistakes: Searching for the first time >= query instead of > query, which is off by one on exact matches.
Re-sorting on every set; appends are already in order.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I keep per-key append-only histories. Set times only increase, so each history is sorted for free, and a get is an upper-bound binary search returning the entry just before the first later time. Sets are O(1) and gets O(log h). If sets could arrive out of order I'd insert in sorted position or use a balanced tree.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: get 4 → first index with time > 4 is 0 → ''. get 5 → index 1 → dark.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: After set light@9: get 8 → index 1 → dark; get 20 → index 2 → light.
